rows.label: classification of matter
rows.correct: A pure substance has fixed composition, whereas a mixture has variable composition and can be separated by physical methods.
wrong: Every homogeneous sample is a pure substance.
rows.explanation: A pure substance has fixed composition, whereas a mixture has variable composition and can be separated by physical methods.

rows.label: SI measurement
rows.correct: A measured physical quantity is reported with a numerical value and an appropriate unit; SI uses seven base units.
wrong: Density and volume are SI base quantities.
rows.explanation: A measured physical quantity is reported with a numerical value and an appropriate unit; SI uses seven base units.

rows.label: density
rows.correct: Density is mass per unit volume.
wrong: Density is volume divided by mass.
rows.explanation: Density is mass per unit volume.

rows.label: temperature conversion
rows.correct: Kelvin temperature equals Celsius temperature plus 273.15.
wrong: A temperature interval of one Celsius degree differs in size from one kelvin.
rows.explanation: Kelvin temperature equals Celsius temperature plus 273.15.

rows.label: significant figures
rows.correct: Significant figures include all certain digits plus the first uncertain digit; leading zeros are not significant.
wrong: Every zero written in a number is significant.
rows.explanation: Significant figures include all certain digits plus the first uncertain digit; leading zeros are not significant.

rows.label: precision and accuracy
rows.correct: Precision concerns repeatability, while accuracy concerns closeness to the accepted value.
wrong: A set of precise readings must be accurate.
rows.explanation: Precision concerns repeatability, while accuracy concerns closeness to the accepted value.

rows.label: scientific notation
rows.correct: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of ten.
wrong: Moving a decimal to the left decreases the power of ten.
rows.explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of ten.

rows.label: dimensional conversion
rows.correct: Unit factors equal one and change the numerical representation without changing the physical quantity.
wrong: The numerical value remains unchanged whenever the unit changes.
rows.explanation: Unit factors equal one and change the numerical representation without changing the physical quantity.

rows.label: law of conservation of mass
rows.correct: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction carried out in a closed system.
wrong: Product mass may be less than reactant mass in a closed vessel because gases have no mass.
rows.explanation: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction carried out in a closed system.

rows.label: law of multiple proportions
rows.correct: When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
wrong: The law compares volumes of all gaseous reactants at arbitrary conditions.
rows.explanation: When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios.

rows.label: average atomic mass
rows.correct: Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of isotopic masses.
wrong: Average atomic mass is the simple mean even when isotope abundances differ.
rows.explanation: Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of isotopic masses.

rows.label: molecular mass
rows.correct: Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
wrong: Subscripts are ignored when adding atomic masses.
rows.explanation: Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.

rows.label: amount of substance
rows.correct: Moles equal sample mass divided by molar mass.
wrong: Moles equal mass multiplied by molar mass.
rows.explanation: Moles equal sample mass divided by molar mass.

rows.label: number of entities
rows.correct: The number of specified entities equals amount in moles times Avogadro constant.
wrong: One mole contains a different number of entities for each substance.
rows.explanation: The number of specified entities equals amount in moles times Avogadro constant.

rows.label: percentage composition
rows.correct: Mass percentage is component mass divided by total mass, multiplied by 100.
wrong: Mass percentage is component mass divided by molar amount.
rows.explanation: Mass percentage is component mass divided by total mass, multiplied by 100.

rows.label: limiting reagent
rows.correct: The limiting reagent is consumed first according to stoichiometric coefficients and fixes the maximum product amount.
wrong: The reactant with the smallest mass is always limiting.
rows.explanation: The limiting reagent is consumed first according to stoichiometric coefficients and fixes the maximum product amount.

rows.label: electron discovery
rows.correct: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles whose charge-to-mass ratio is independent of electrode material.
wrong: Cathode-ray properties depend completely on the gas and electrodes used.
rows.explanation: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles whose charge-to-mass ratio is independent of electrode material.

rows.label: Rutherford nuclear model
rows.correct: Most alpha particles passed undeflected, showing that atoms are mostly empty space; rare large deflections revealed a small positive nucleus.
wrong: Large deflections showed positive charge spread uniformly through the atom.
rows.explanation: Most alpha particles passed undeflected, showing that atoms are mostly empty space; rare large deflections revealed a small positive nucleus.

rows.label: mass number
rows.correct: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
wrong: Mass number equals the number of neutrons only.
rows.explanation: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.

rows.label: charge from elementary charges
rows.correct: Net charge is the algebraic sum of integer multiples of elementary charge.
wrong: Removing an electron makes an atom negatively charged.
rows.explanation: Net charge is the algebraic sum of integer multiples of elementary charge.

rows.label: electromagnetic spectrum
rows.correct: All electromagnetic radiation travels at c in vacuum and satisfies c = νλ.
wrong: Higher frequency radiation has a longer wavelength in vacuum.
rows.explanation: All electromagnetic radiation travels at c in vacuum and satisfies c = νλ.

rows.label: line spectrum
rows.correct: Atomic line spectra contain discrete frequencies, indicating quantised energy changes.
wrong: A hydrogen line spectrum is continuous because electron energy is unrestricted.
rows.explanation: Atomic line spectra contain discrete frequencies, indicating quantised energy changes.

rows.label: frequency-wavelength relation
rows.correct: Frequency equals the speed of light divided by wavelength.
wrong: Frequency is directly proportional to wavelength in vacuum.
rows.explanation: Frequency equals the speed of light divided by wavelength.

rows.label: photon energy
rows.correct: Photon energy is Planck constant times frequency.
wrong: Photon energy is inversely proportional to frequency.
rows.explanation: Photon energy is Planck constant times frequency.

rows.label: Bohr quantisation
rows.correct: In a permitted stationary orbit an electron has definite energy and does not radiate; radiation accompanies transitions.
wrong: An electron radiates continuously while remaining in a stationary orbit.
rows.explanation: In a permitted stationary orbit an electron has definite energy and does not radiate; radiation accompanies transitions.

rows.label: uncertainty principle
rows.correct: Position and momentum cannot both be known simultaneously with unlimited precision.
wrong: Uncertainty arises only from poor instruments and vanishes with perfect apparatus.
rows.explanation: Position and momentum cannot both be known simultaneously with unlimited precision.

rows.label: Bohr energy
rows.correct: For hydrogen, energy of level n is -13.6/n² eV.
wrong: Bohr energy is proportional to n² and remains negative with increasing magnitude.
rows.explanation: For hydrogen, energy of level n is -13.6/n² eV.

rows.label: de Broglie wavelength
rows.correct: Matter wavelength equals Planck constant divided by momentum.
wrong: Matter wavelength is directly proportional to momentum.
rows.explanation: Matter wavelength equals Planck constant divided by momentum.

rows.label: quantum numbers
rows.correct: For a given n, l ranges from 0 to n-1 and mₗ ranges from -l to +l.
wrong: For n = 2, l may equal 2.
rows.explanation: For a given n, l ranges from 0 to n-1 and mₗ ranges from -l to +l.

rows.label: filling principles
rows.correct: Aufbau gives increasing-energy filling, Pauli limits an orbital to two opposite-spin electrons, and Hund maximises unpaired electrons in degenerate orbitals.
wrong: Hund pairing occurs before each degenerate orbital is singly occupied.
rows.explanation: Aufbau gives increasing-energy filling, Pauli limits an orbital to two opposite-spin electrons, and Hund maximises unpaired electrons in degenerate orbitals.

rows.label: orbitals in a subshell
rows.correct: A subshell of azimuthal quantum number l contains 2l+1 orbitals.
wrong: Every subshell contains n² orbitals.
rows.explanation: A subshell of azimuthal quantum number l contains 2l+1 orbitals.

rows.label: maximum electrons in a shell
rows.correct: A shell with principal quantum number n can hold at most 2n² electrons.
wrong: A shell can hold at most n² electrons.
rows.explanation: A shell with principal quantum number n can hold at most 2n² electrons.

chapters.name: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

rows.label: modern periodic law
rows.correct: Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number.
wrong: Modern periodic law arranges elements strictly by atomic mass.
rows.explanation: Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number.

rows.label: Mendeleev table
rows.correct: Mendeleev left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements using periodic trends.
wrong: Mendeleev’s table could assign isotopes to distinct positions without difficulty.
rows.explanation: Mendeleev left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements using periodic trends.

rows.label: period length
rows.correct: A period length reflects the number of electrons accommodated in subshells filled across it.
wrong: Every period contains exactly eight elements.
rows.explanation: A period length reflects the number of electrons accommodated in subshells filled across it.

rows.label: atomic number interval
rows.correct: Atomic number increases by one for each successive element.
wrong: Atomic number may decrease within a period.
rows.explanation: Atomic number increases by one for each successive element.

rows.label: block assignment
rows.correct: The subshell receiving the differentiating electron identifies the s, p, d or f block.
wrong: The highest principal quantum number alone always identifies the block.
rows.explanation: The subshell receiving the differentiating electron identifies the s, p, d or f block.

rows.label: group configuration
rows.correct: Main-group elements in one group share a similar valence-shell configuration and therefore related chemical behaviour.
wrong: All elements in a period have the same valence-shell configuration.
rows.explanation: Main-group elements in one group share a similar valence-shell configuration and therefore related chemical behaviour.

rows.label: period from configuration
rows.correct: For a main-group element, the highest occupied principal quantum number gives its period.
wrong: The number of valence electrons always gives the period.
rows.explanation: For a main-group element, the highest occupied principal quantum number gives its period.

rows.label: main-group valence electrons
rows.correct: For p-block groups 13–18, group number minus ten gives the usual valence-electron count.
wrong: Group number itself equals the p-block valence-electron count.
rows.explanation: For p-block groups 13–18, group number minus ten gives the usual valence-electron count.

rows.label: atomic radius trend
rows.correct: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because effective nuclear charge rises, and increases down a group as shells are added.
wrong: Atomic radius generally increases from left to right across a period.
rows.explanation: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because effective nuclear charge rises, and increases down a group as shells are added.

rows.label: ionic size
rows.correct: A cation is smaller than its parent atom, while an anion is larger, because electron loss or gain changes attraction and repulsion.
wrong: A cation is always larger than its neutral atom.
rows.explanation: A cation is smaller than its parent atom, while an anion is larger, because electron loss or gain changes attraction and repulsion.

rows.label: isoelectronic electron count
rows.correct: Isoelectronic species contain the same number of electrons.
wrong: Isoelectronic species must have the same nuclear charge.
rows.explanation: Isoelectronic species contain the same number of electrons.

rows.label: effective nuclear attraction proxy
rows.correct: Within an isoelectronic series, greater nuclear charge generally gives smaller radius.
wrong: Within an isoelectronic series, radius grows with nuclear charge.
rows.explanation: Within an isoelectronic series, greater nuclear charge generally gives smaller radius.

rows.label: ionisation enthalpy
rows.correct: Ionisation enthalpy generally rises across a period and falls down a group, with configuration-based exceptions.
wrong: Shielding decreases strongly down a group, so ionisation enthalpy rises.
rows.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy generally rises across a period and falls down a group, with configuration-based exceptions.

rows.label: electron gain and electronegativity
rows.correct: Electron gain enthalpy describes adding an electron to an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity describes attraction for shared electrons in a bond.
wrong: Electronegativity is an enthalpy measured for an isolated atom.
rows.explanation: Electron gain enthalpy describes adding an electron to an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity describes attraction for shared electrons in a bond.

rows.label: successive ionisation jump
rows.correct: A large jump after removal of valence electrons indicates entry into a stable inner shell.
wrong: Successive ionisation enthalpies normally decrease.
rows.explanation: A large jump after removal of valence electrons indicates entry into a stable inner shell.

rows.label: electronegativity difference
rows.correct: Bond polarity often increases with the magnitude of electronegativity difference.
wrong: Electronegativity difference keeps a negative sign and polarity decreases with magnitude.
rows.explanation: Bond polarity often increases with the magnitude of electronegativity difference.

rows.label: Lewis symbols and octet
rows.correct: Lewis symbols display valence electrons; many main-group atoms bond to approach a noble-gas configuration.
wrong: The octet rule has no exceptions and applies literally to every molecule.
rows.explanation: Lewis symbols display valence electrons; many main-group atoms bond to approach a noble-gas configuration.

rows.label: ionic bond formation
rows.correct: Ionic bonding reflects electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions and is favoured by the overall energetics of ion formation and lattice creation.
wrong: An electron-transfer step alone guarantees a stable ionic solid regardless of energy.
rows.explanation: Ionic bonding reflects electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions and is favoured by the overall energetics of ion formation and lattice creation.

rows.label: formal charge
rows.correct: Formal charge assigns bonding electrons equally between bonded atoms.
wrong: Formal charge assigns all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom.
rows.explanation: Formal charge assigns bonding electrons equally between bonded atoms.

rows.label: lattice stoichiometry
rows.correct: Electrical neutrality requires total positive and negative charge to balance in an ionic formula.
wrong: Ionic subscripts are chosen from atomic masses.
rows.explanation: Electrical neutrality requires total positive and negative charge to balance in an ionic formula.

rows.label: bond order and length
rows.correct: For comparable atoms, higher bond order generally means a shorter, stronger bond.
wrong: A triple bond is generally longer and weaker than a single bond.
rows.explanation: For comparable atoms, higher bond order generally means a shorter, stronger bond.

rows.label: resonance
rows.correct: A resonance hybrid is the actual delocalised structure and is more stable than any single canonical form.
wrong: Canonical resonance forms rapidly interconvert as separate molecules.
rows.explanation: A resonance hybrid is the actual delocalised structure and is more stable than any single canonical form.

rows.label: dipole moment
rows.correct: Dipole moment magnitude is charge times separation.
wrong: Dipole moment is charge divided by separation.
rows.explanation: Dipole moment magnitude is charge times separation.

rows.label: average resonance bond order
rows.correct: Equivalent resonance bonds can have a fractional average bond order.
wrong: Every bond in a resonance hybrid must have integral bond order.
rows.explanation: Equivalent resonance bonds can have a fractional average bond order.

rows.label: electron-pair repulsion
rows.correct: VSEPR repulsions follow lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
wrong: Bond pairs repel more strongly than lone pairs because they lie closer to the central atom.
rows.explanation: VSEPR repulsions follow lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

rows.label: shape versus geometry
rows.correct: Electron-pair geometry counts all electron domains, while molecular shape describes positions of atoms.
wrong: Lone pairs are included as atoms when naming molecular shape.
rows.explanation: Electron-pair geometry counts all electron domains, while molecular shape describes positions of atoms.

rows.label: steric number
rows.correct: Steric number is the number of sigma-bond domains plus lone pairs on the central atom.
wrong: Pi bonds are counted as separate electron domains in VSEPR.
rows.explanation: Steric number is the number of sigma-bond domains plus lone pairs on the central atom.

rows.label: ideal bond-pair count
rows.correct: A molecule with n terminal atoms joined by sigma bonds has n central bond domains before lone pairs are added.
wrong: A double bond creates two directional domains.
rows.explanation: A molecule with n terminal atoms joined by sigma bonds has n central bond domains before lone pairs are added.

rows.label: sigma and pi bonds
rows.correct: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap about the internuclear axis; a pi bond forms by sidewise overlap above and below it.
wrong: Free rotation is easier about a pi bond than about a sigma bond.
rows.explanation: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap about the internuclear axis; a pi bond forms by sidewise overlap above and below it.

rows.label: hybridisation
rows.correct: Hybrid orbitals are equivalent directed combinations of atomic orbitals used to describe molecular geometry.
wrong: Hybridisation is a physical mixing of different atoms before bonding.
rows.explanation: Hybrid orbitals are equivalent directed combinations of atomic orbitals used to describe molecular geometry.

rows.label: sigma bond count
rows.correct: A connected molecular skeleton has one sigma bond for every directly bonded atom pair, including within multiple bonds.
wrong: A double bond contains two sigma bonds.
rows.explanation: A connected molecular skeleton has one sigma bond for every directly bonded atom pair, including within multiple bonds.

rows.label: hybrid orbital count
rows.correct: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed.
wrong: Mixing one s and three p orbitals gives three hybrids.
rows.explanation: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed.

rows.label: molecular orbitals
rows.correct: Constructive combination forms a lower-energy bonding MO; destructive combination forms a higher-energy antibonding MO.
wrong: Bonding and antibonding orbitals have identical electron density between nuclei.
rows.explanation: Constructive combination forms a lower-energy bonding MO; destructive combination forms a higher-energy antibonding MO.

rows.label: magnetic behaviour
rows.correct: A molecule is paramagnetic if its MO configuration contains unpaired electrons.
wrong: O2 is diamagnetic because all valence electrons pair.
rows.explanation: A molecule is paramagnetic if its MO configuration contains unpaired electrons.

rows.label: MO bond order
rows.correct: MO bond order is half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons.
wrong: Bond order is the sum of bonding and antibonding electrons.
rows.explanation: MO bond order is half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons.

rows.label: unpaired-electron magnetic moment
rows.correct: The spin-only moment is approximately √[n(n+2)] Bohr magnetons for n unpaired electrons.
wrong: Magnetic moment is simply n².
rows.explanation: The spin-only moment is approximately √[n(n+2)] Bohr magnetons for n unpaired electrons.

rows.label: hydrogen bond
rows.correct: A hydrogen bond forms when H bonded to a highly electronegative atom interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
wrong: Every compound containing hydrogen forms strong hydrogen bonds.
rows.explanation: A hydrogen bond forms when H bonded to a highly electronegative atom interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.

rows.label: intermolecular versus intramolecular
rows.correct: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding associates molecules, while intramolecular bonding occurs within one molecule and can reduce intermolecular association.
wrong: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding always raises water solubility.
rows.explanation: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding associates molecules, while intramolecular bonding occurs within one molecule and can reduce intermolecular association.

rows.label: hydrogen-bond donor count
rows.correct: A donor site requires a hydrogen directly attached to an electronegative atom such as N, O or F.
wrong: Every lone pair is a hydrogen-bond donor.
rows.explanation: A donor site requires a hydrogen directly attached to an electronegative atom such as N, O or F.

rows.label: hydrogen-bond acceptor count
rows.correct: A typical acceptor site is an available lone pair on an electronegative atom.
wrong: A positively charged proton has a lone pair and is an acceptor.
rows.explanation: A typical acceptor site is an available lone pair on an electronegative atom.

rows.label: thermodynamic system
rows.correct: An open system exchanges matter and energy, a closed system exchanges energy but not matter, and an isolated system exchanges neither.
wrong: A closed system cannot exchange heat or work.
rows.explanation: An open system exchanges matter and energy, a closed system exchanges energy but not matter, and an isolated system exchanges neither.

rows.label: state functions
rows.correct: A state function depends only on the thermodynamic state, not the path; heat and work are path functions.
wrong: Heat and work are stored state properties of a system.
rows.explanation: A state function depends only on the thermodynamic state, not the path; heat and work are path functions.

rows.label: internal-energy change
rows.correct: The change in internal energy is final value minus initial value.
wrong: Internal-energy change depends on the route between states.
rows.explanation: The change in internal energy is final value minus initial value.

rows.label: cyclic process
rows.correct: A state function has zero net change over a complete cycle.
wrong: Heat and work must each be zero for every cycle.
rows.explanation: A state function has zero net change over a complete cycle.

rows.label: first law sign convention
rows.correct: With the chemistry convention, ΔU = q + w and work done on the system is positive.
wrong: Expansion work done by the system is positive in ΔU = q + w.
rows.explanation: With the chemistry convention, ΔU = q + w and work done on the system is positive.

rows.label: enthalpy
rows.correct: Enthalpy is H = U + pV; at constant pressure under appropriate conditions, heat exchanged equals ΔH.
wrong: Enthalpy is heat contained in a body and is a path function.
rows.explanation: Enthalpy is H = U + pV; at constant pressure under appropriate conditions, heat exchanged equals ΔH.

rows.label: first law
rows.correct: Internal-energy change equals heat supplied plus work done on the system.
wrong: Heat and work have fixed values determined only by endpoints.
rows.explanation: Internal-energy change equals heat supplied plus work done on the system.

rows.label: expansion work
rows.correct: Against constant external pressure, pressure-volume work is -PextΔV.
wrong: Expansion work is positive under the chemistry sign convention.
rows.explanation: Against constant external pressure, pressure-volume work is -PextΔV.

rows.label: heat capacity
rows.correct: Heat capacity is heat required for a unit temperature rise; specific heat capacity refers to unit mass.
wrong: Specific heat capacity increases automatically with sample mass.
rows.explanation: Heat capacity is heat required for a unit temperature rise; specific heat capacity refers to unit mass.

rows.label: calorimeter energy balance
rows.correct: In an ideally insulated calorimeter, heat lost by hotter parts equals heat gained by cooler parts.
wrong: Both hot and cold bodies gain heat until equilibrium.
rows.explanation: In an ideally insulated calorimeter, heat lost by hotter parts equals heat gained by cooler parts.

rows.label: sensible heat
rows.correct: For constant specific heat, q = mcΔT.
wrong: Heat is proportional to final temperature rather than temperature change.
rows.explanation: For constant specific heat, q = mcΔT.

rows.label: molar heat capacity
rows.correct: Heat equals amount times molar heat capacity times temperature change.
wrong: Molar heat capacity has units per kilogram.
rows.explanation: Heat equals amount times molar heat capacity times temperature change.

rows.label: Hess law
rows.correct: Reaction enthalpy is independent of path, so thermochemical equations may be added after reversing or scaling them with corresponding ΔH changes.
wrong: Reversing a reaction leaves the sign of ΔH unchanged.
rows.explanation: Reaction enthalpy is independent of path, so thermochemical equations may be added after reversing or scaling them with corresponding ΔH changes.

rows.label: standard formation enthalpy
rows.correct: Standard formation enthalpy forms one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states; an element in its standard state has value zero.
wrong: Every elemental allotrope has zero formation enthalpy under the same conditions.
rows.explanation: Standard formation enthalpy forms one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states; an element in its standard state has value zero.

rows.label: reaction enthalpy from formation data
rows.correct: Reaction enthalpy is the stoichiometric sum for products minus that for reactants.
wrong: Reactant formation enthalpies are added rather than subtracted.
rows.explanation: Reaction enthalpy is the stoichiometric sum for products minus that for reactants.

rows.label: bond enthalpy estimate
rows.correct: Using average bond enthalpies, ΔH is bonds broken minus bonds formed.
wrong: Bond formation absorbs energy while bond breaking releases it.
rows.explanation: Using average bond enthalpies, ΔH is bonds broken minus bonds formed.

rows.label: spontaneity
rows.correct: A spontaneous process is thermodynamically feasible under stated conditions but need not be fast.
wrong: Every spontaneous reaction is instantaneous.
rows.explanation: A spontaneous process is thermodynamically feasible under stated conditions but need not be fast.

rows.label: entropy
rows.correct: Entropy measures dispersal of energy or number of accessible arrangements; an isolated system tends toward greater total entropy in a spontaneous process.
wrong: The entropy of the system must decrease in every spontaneous process.
rows.explanation: Entropy measures dispersal of energy or number of accessible arrangements; an isolated system tends toward greater total entropy in a spontaneous process.

rows.label: Gibbs energy
rows.correct: At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS and a negative ΔG indicates spontaneity.
wrong: A positive ΔG indicates a spontaneous forward process.
rows.explanation: At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS and a negative ΔG indicates spontaneity.

rows.label: equilibrium temperature
rows.correct: When ΔH and ΔS are treated as constant, ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS.
wrong: Equilibrium temperature equals ΔH multiplied by ΔS.
rows.explanation: When ΔH and ΔS are treated as constant, ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS.

rows.label: dynamic physical equilibrium
rows.correct: At equilibrium opposing microscopic processes continue at equal rates while macroscopic properties remain constant.
wrong: Equilibrium means all molecular motion has stopped.
rows.explanation: At equilibrium opposing microscopic processes continue at equal rates while macroscopic properties remain constant.

rows.label: saturated solution
rows.correct: In a saturated solution at fixed temperature, dissolution and crystallisation occur at equal rates.
wrong: A saturated solution contains no undissolved solute under any condition.
rows.explanation: In a saturated solution at fixed temperature, dissolution and crystallisation occur at equal rates.

rows.label: vapour-pressure ratio
rows.correct: At equilibrium a fixed-temperature liquid has a characteristic vapour pressure.
wrong: Equilibrium vapour pressure grows indefinitely with vessel volume.
rows.explanation: At equilibrium a fixed-temperature liquid has a characteristic vapour pressure.

rows.label: Henry-law concentration proxy
rows.correct: At fixed temperature, gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure in the dilute regime.
wrong: Gas solubility is inversely proportional to partial pressure.
rows.explanation: At fixed temperature, gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure in the dilute regime.

rows.label: law of mass action
rows.correct: For a balanced reaction, the equilibrium constant uses activities or concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers.
wrong: Pure solids must always appear as concentration terms in Kc.
rows.explanation: For a balanced reaction, the equilibrium constant uses activities or concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers.

rows.label: meaning of K
rows.correct: At a fixed temperature, large K favours products at equilibrium, while K does not by itself state how fast equilibrium is reached.
wrong: A large K guarantees a fast reaction.
rows.explanation: At a fixed temperature, large K favours products at equilibrium, while K does not by itself state how fast equilibrium is reached.

rows.label: simple equilibrium constant
rows.correct: For A ⇌ B, Kc is [B]/[A] at equilibrium.
wrong: Kc uses initial concentrations instead of equilibrium concentrations.
rows.explanation: For A ⇌ B, Kc is [B]/[A] at equilibrium.

rows.label: relation between Kp and Kc
rows.correct: For gaseous reactions, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn where Δn is gaseous product moles minus gaseous reactant moles.
wrong: Δn includes pure liquids and solids.
rows.explanation: For gaseous reactions, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn where Δn is gaseous product moles minus gaseous reactant moles.

rows.label: reaction quotient
rows.correct: Q has the same form as K but uses current composition; Q < K drives the forward direction and Q > K drives reverse.
wrong: Q can be calculated only at equilibrium.
rows.explanation: Q has the same form as K but uses current composition; Q < K drives the forward direction and Q > K drives reverse.

rows.label: Gibbs energy and equilibrium
rows.correct: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K.
wrong: At equilibrium ΔG° must always be zero.
rows.explanation: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K.

rows.label: standard Gibbs energy from K
rows.correct: Standard Gibbs energy is -RT ln K.
wrong: A large K gives a positive ΔG°.
rows.explanation: Standard Gibbs energy is -RT ln K.

rows.label: quotient comparison
rows.correct: The ratio Q/K immediately indicates the required direction.
wrong: Q/K below one requires net reverse reaction.
rows.explanation: The ratio Q/K immediately indicates the required direction.

rows.label: concentration and pressure effects
rows.correct: An equilibrium shifts to oppose a concentration change; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles when gas mole counts differ.
wrong: A catalyst changes equilibrium composition toward products.
rows.explanation: An equilibrium shifts to oppose a concentration change; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles when gas mole counts differ.

rows.label: temperature effect
rows.correct: Temperature changes K; heating favours the endothermic direction and cooling favours the exothermic direction.
wrong: Changing pressure always changes the numerical value of K.
rows.explanation: Temperature changes K; heating favours the endothermic direction and cooling favours the exothermic direction.

rows.label: gas mole change
rows.correct: Pressure-shift direction depends on the difference in gaseous stoichiometric moles.
wrong: Solids are counted when deciding a pressure shift.
rows.explanation: Pressure-shift direction depends on the difference in gaseous stoichiometric moles.

rows.label: dilution factor
rows.correct: On dilution, all solute concentrations fall by the volume-increase factor before equilibrium readjusts.
wrong: Dilution initially increases every solute concentration.
rows.explanation: On dilution, all solute concentrations fall by the volume-increase factor before equilibrium readjusts.

rows.label: Brønsted acids and bases
rows.correct: A Brønsted acid donates a proton and a Brønsted base accepts one; conjugate pairs differ by one proton.
wrong: A Brønsted base must contain hydroxide ion.
rows.explanation: A Brønsted acid donates a proton and a Brønsted base accepts one; conjugate pairs differ by one proton.

rows.label: Lewis acids and bases
rows.correct: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates an electron pair.
wrong: A Lewis acid must donate H+.
rows.explanation: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates an electron pair.

rows.label: acid dissociation constant
rows.correct: For HA ⇌ H+ + A-, Ka is [H+][A-]/[HA] under the usual dilute-solution convention.
wrong: A stronger acid has a smaller Ka.
rows.explanation: For HA ⇌ H+ + A-, Ka is [H+][A-]/[HA] under the usual dilute-solution convention.

rows.label: degree of ionisation
rows.correct: Degree of ionisation is amount ionised divided by initial amount.
wrong: Degree of ionisation may exceed one for a simple monoprotic acid.
rows.explanation: Degree of ionisation is amount ionised divided by initial amount.

rows.label: ionic product of water
rows.correct: At 298 K, Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1.0 × 10^-14 in dilute aqueous solution.
wrong: Neutral water always has pH 7 at every temperature.
rows.explanation: At 298 K, Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1.0 × 10^-14 in dilute aqueous solution.

rows.label: common-ion effect
rows.correct: A common ion suppresses ionisation of a weak electrolyte by shifting its equilibrium.
wrong: Adding a common ion increases weak-acid ionisation.
rows.explanation: A common ion suppresses ionisation of a weak electrolyte by shifting its equilibrium.

rows.label: pH
rows.correct: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration.
wrong: pH equals log[H+] without a negative sign.
rows.explanation: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration.

rows.label: weak-acid approximation
rows.correct: For a weak monoprotic acid with small ionisation, [H+] ≈ √(KaC).
wrong: Weak-acid [H+] always equals its analytical concentration.
rows.explanation: For a weak monoprotic acid with small ionisation, [H+] ≈ √(KaC).

rows.label: buffer action
rows.correct: A buffer contains a weak acid/base and its conjugate partner and resists small additions of acid or base.
wrong: A buffer keeps pH exactly constant after unlimited acid addition.
rows.explanation: A buffer contains a weak acid/base and its conjugate partner and resists small additions of acid or base.

rows.label: solubility product
rows.correct: Ksp is the product of equilibrium ion concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers for a sparingly soluble salt.
wrong: Ksp equals molar solubility for every salt stoichiometry.
rows.explanation: Ksp is the product of equilibrium ion concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers for a sparingly soluble salt.

rows.label: Henderson relation
rows.correct: For an acidic buffer, pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) under the standard approximation.
wrong: Equal acid and conjugate-base concentrations give pH zero.
rows.explanation: For an acidic buffer, pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) under the standard approximation.

rows.label: 1:1 salt solubility
rows.correct: For a 1:1 salt AB, Ksp = s² when molar solubility is s in pure water.
wrong: For every salt, Ksp equals s.
rows.explanation: For a 1:1 salt AB, Ksp = s² when molar solubility is s in pure water.

rows.label: oxidation by oxygen transfer
rows.correct: Oxidation includes addition of oxygen to a substance, as in 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.
wrong: Oxidation always means removal of oxygen.
rows.explanation: Oxidation includes addition of oxygen to a substance, as in 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.

rows.label: reduction by oxygen transfer
rows.correct: Reduction includes removal of oxygen, as when CuO is converted to Cu by hydrogen.
wrong: A substance that loses oxygen is oxidised.
rows.explanation: Reduction includes removal of oxygen, as when CuO is converted to Cu by hydrogen.

rows.label: oxidation by hydrogen transfer
rows.correct: Removal of hydrogen is oxidation, whereas addition of hydrogen is reduction.
wrong: Addition of hydrogen is oxidation.
rows.explanation: Removal of hydrogen is oxidation, whereas addition of hydrogen is reduction.

rows.label: oxidising and reducing agents
rows.correct: An oxidising agent causes oxidation and is itself reduced; a reducing agent causes reduction and is itself oxidised.
wrong: An oxidising agent must itself be oxidised.
rows.explanation: An oxidising agent causes oxidation and is itself reduced; a reducing agent causes reduction and is itself oxidised.

rows.label: oxidation as electron loss
rows.correct: Oxidation is loss of electrons; Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- is an oxidation half-reaction.
wrong: Electron gain is oxidation.
rows.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons; Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- is an oxidation half-reaction.

rows.label: reduction as electron gain
rows.correct: Reduction is gain of electrons; Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu is a reduction half-reaction.
wrong: A cation is reduced by losing electrons.
rows.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons; Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu is a reduction half-reaction.

rows.label: competitive electron transfer
rows.correct: A metal that more readily loses electrons can reduce ions of a less reactive metal from solution.
wrong: Any metal displaces every other metal ion from solution.
rows.explanation: A metal that more readily loses electrons can reduce ions of a less reactive metal from solution.

rows.label: redox conjugate pair
rows.correct: The oxidised and reduced forms connected by electron transfer constitute a redox couple, such as Zn2+/Zn.
wrong: A redox couple contains unrelated elements.
rows.explanation: The oxidised and reduced forms connected by electron transfer constitute a redox couple, such as Zn2+/Zn.

rows.label: oxidation-number sum rule
rows.correct: The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers is zero in a neutral compound and equals the ionic charge in a polyatomic ion.
wrong: The sum is always zero, even for a charged ion.
rows.explanation: The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers is zero in a neutral compound and equals the ionic charge in a polyatomic ion.

rows.label: oxygen exceptions
rows.correct: Oxygen is usually -2, is -1 in peroxides, -1/2 on average in superoxides, and positive when bonded to fluorine.
wrong: Oxygen is -2 in every compound without exception.
rows.explanation: Oxygen is usually -2, is -1 in peroxides, -1/2 on average in superoxides, and positive when bonded to fluorine.

rows.label: hydrogen and fluorine rules
rows.correct: Hydrogen is usually +1 but -1 in metal hydrides; fluorine is -1 in all its compounds.
wrong: Hydrogen is always +1 and fluorine can be positive.
rows.explanation: Hydrogen is usually +1 but -1 in metal hydrides; fluorine is -1 in all its compounds.

rows.label: fractional oxidation number
rows.correct: A fractional oxidation number is an average value and need not be the actual state of every equivalent-looking atom.
wrong: Every atom in a mixed-valence compound physically has the same fractional charge.
rows.explanation: A fractional oxidation number is an average value and need not be the actual state of every equivalent-looking atom.

rows.label: combination redox reaction
rows.correct: A combination redox reaction forms one product while oxidation numbers of participating elements change.
wrong: Every combination reaction is necessarily redox.
rows.explanation: A combination redox reaction forms one product while oxidation numbers of participating elements change.

rows.label: decomposition redox reaction
rows.correct: A decomposition is redox only if at least one element is oxidised and another is reduced.
wrong: All thermal decompositions are redox reactions.
rows.explanation: A decomposition is redox only if at least one element is oxidised and another is reduced.

rows.label: displacement redox reaction
rows.correct: In a displacement redox reaction, an atom or ion replaces another because electron transfer is favourable.
wrong: Displacement occurs without any oxidation-state change.
rows.explanation: In a displacement redox reaction, an atom or ion replaces another because electron transfer is favourable.

rows.label: disproportionation
rows.correct: In disproportionation, the same species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced to products with higher and lower oxidation states.
wrong: Disproportionation gives products having identical oxidation states.
rows.explanation: In disproportionation, the same species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced to products with higher and lower oxidation states.

rows.label: oxidation-number method
rows.correct: Total increase in oxidation number must equal total decrease before the remaining atoms and charge are balanced.
wrong: Oxidation-number increases and decreases may be balanced independently.
rows.explanation: Total increase in oxidation number must equal total decrease before the remaining atoms and charge are balanced.

rows.label: ion-electron method in acid
rows.correct: In acidic medium, balance O with H2O, H with H+, charge with electrons, then equalise and cancel electrons.
wrong: Oxygen is balanced with OH- first in acidic medium.
rows.explanation: In acidic medium, balance O with H2O, H with H+, charge with electrons, then equalise and cancel electrons.

rows.label: ion-electron method in base
rows.correct: A basic-medium equation may be balanced using H2O and OH-, or first in acid followed by neutralising H+ with OH-.
wrong: H+ must remain in the final basic-medium equation.
rows.explanation: A basic-medium equation may be balanced using H2O and OH-, or first in acid followed by neutralising H+ with OH-.

rows.label: mass-and-charge audit
rows.correct: A correctly balanced ionic redox equation has equal numbers of each atom and equal net charge on both sides.
wrong: Matching atoms alone proves that an ionic equation is balanced.
rows.explanation: A correctly balanced ionic redox equation has equal numbers of each atom and equal net charge on both sides.

rows.label: redox titration equivalence
rows.correct: At equivalence, oxidant and reductant have reacted in the stoichiometric electron ratio of the balanced equation.
wrong: Equal solution volumes always mark equivalence.
rows.explanation: At equivalence, oxidant and reductant have reacted in the stoichiometric electron ratio of the balanced equation.

rows.label: oxidation-number limitation
rows.correct: Oxidation number is a formal electron-bookkeeping device and is not always the actual charge on an atom.
wrong: Oxidation number and covalent atomic charge are always identical.
rows.explanation: Oxidation number is a formal electron-bookkeeping device and is not always the actual charge on an atom.

rows.label: anode process
rows.correct: Oxidation occurs at the anode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.
wrong: Reduction occurs at the anode because the anode is always negative.
rows.explanation: Oxidation occurs at the anode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

rows.label: cathode process
rows.correct: Reduction occurs at the cathode; electrons are consumed by the species being reduced.
wrong: The cathode is defined as the electrode where oxidation occurs.
rows.explanation: Reduction occurs at the cathode; electrons are consumed by the species being reduced.

chapters.name: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

rows.label: carbon tetravalence
rows.correct: Carbon normally forms four covalent bonds because it has four valence electrons and attains an octet by sharing.
wrong: Neutral carbon normally forms only two covalent bonds.
rows.explanation: Carbon normally forms four covalent bonds because it has four valence electrons and attains an octet by sharing.

rows.label: sp3 hybridisation
rows.correct: An sp3 carbon has four equivalent hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally with an ideal angle near 109.5 degrees.
wrong: sp3 carbon is trigonal planar with a 120 degree angle.
rows.explanation: An sp3 carbon has four equivalent hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally with an ideal angle near 109.5 degrees.

rows.label: sp2 and sp hybridisation
rows.correct: sp2 gives trigonal-planar geometry with one unhybridised p orbital; sp gives linear geometry with two unhybridised p orbitals.
wrong: sp carbon is tetrahedral and has no unhybridised p orbital.
rows.explanation: sp2 gives trigonal-planar geometry with one unhybridised p orbital; sp gives linear geometry with two unhybridised p orbitals.

rows.label: sigma and pi bonding
rows.correct: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap, while a pi bond forms by sidewise overlap of parallel orbitals.
wrong: A double bond contains two pi bonds and no sigma bond.
rows.explanation: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap, while a pi bond forms by sidewise overlap of parallel orbitals.

rows.label: complete structural formula
rows.correct: A complete structural formula shows all atoms and covalent bonds explicitly.
wrong: A complete formula omits all carbon-hydrogen bonds.
rows.explanation: A complete structural formula shows all atoms and covalent bonds explicitly.

rows.label: condensed formula
rows.correct: A condensed formula groups atoms while preserving their connectivity, for example CH3CH2OH.
wrong: A condensed formula uniquely displays every bond angle and stereochemical direction.
rows.explanation: A condensed formula groups atoms while preserving their connectivity, for example CH3CH2OH.

rows.label: bond-line notation
rows.correct: In bond-line notation, line ends and vertices represent carbon atoms and hydrogens on carbon are usually omitted.
wrong: Every vertex represents a hydrogen atom.
rows.explanation: In bond-line notation, line ends and vertices represent carbon atoms and hydrogens on carbon are usually omitted.

rows.label: wedge-dash representation
rows.correct: A solid wedge projects toward the viewer, a dashed wedge projects behind the plane, and ordinary lines lie in the plane.
wrong: Wedge and dash symbols indicate different bond orders.
rows.explanation: A solid wedge projects toward the viewer, a dashed wedge projects behind the plane, and ordinary lines lie in the plane.

rows.label: acyclic and cyclic classification
rows.correct: Open-chain compounds are acyclic; ring compounds are cyclic and may be homocyclic or heterocyclic.
wrong: Every cyclic compound is aromatic.
rows.explanation: Open-chain compounds are acyclic; ring compounds are cyclic and may be homocyclic or heterocyclic.

rows.label: aromatic and aliphatic compounds
rows.correct: Aromatic compounds meet structural and electron-delocalisation requirements; aliphatic compounds need not contain a benzene ring.
wrong: Every unsaturated cyclic compound is aromatic.
rows.explanation: Aromatic compounds meet structural and electron-delocalisation requirements; aliphatic compounds need not contain a benzene ring.

rows.label: functional group
rows.correct: A functional group is an atom or group that largely determines a characteristic set of reactions of an organic compound.
wrong: The longest carbon chain itself is always the functional group.
rows.explanation: A functional group is an atom or group that largely determines a characteristic set of reactions of an organic compound.

rows.label: homologous series
rows.correct: Successive members of a homologous series differ by CH2 and share a functional group and general chemical properties.
wrong: Successive homologues differ by CH3 and have identical physical constants.
rows.explanation: Successive members of a homologous series differ by CH2 and share a functional group and general chemical properties.

rows.label: principal functional group
rows.correct: The principal functional group determines the suffix and must receive the lowest permissible locant under the applicable priority rules.
wrong: Alphabetical order alone determines the principal suffix.
rows.explanation: The principal functional group determines the suffix and must receive the lowest permissible locant under the applicable priority rules.

rows.label: parent-chain selection
rows.correct: The parent chain must include the principal functional group and the maximum number of multiple bonds before length tie-breakers are applied.
wrong: The visually straightest chain is always the parent.
rows.explanation: The parent chain must include the principal functional group and the maximum number of multiple bonds before length tie-breakers are applied.

rows.label: lowest set of locants
rows.correct: Numbering follows the lowest-set and first-point-of-difference rules after satisfying principal-group and multiple-bond priorities.
wrong: Locants are chosen to minimise the alphabetically first substituent before the suffix group.
rows.explanation: Numbering follows the lowest-set and first-point-of-difference rules after satisfying principal-group and multiple-bond priorities.

rows.label: substituent ordering
rows.correct: Different substituent prefixes are cited alphabetically; multiplicative prefixes such as di and tri are ignored for alphabetisation.
wrong: Substituents are listed from highest locant to lowest locant.
rows.explanation: Different substituent prefixes are cited alphabetically; multiplicative prefixes such as di and tri are ignored for alphabetisation.

rows.label: chain isomerism
rows.correct: Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons.
wrong: Chain isomers differ only by rotation about a single bond.
rows.explanation: Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons.

rows.label: position isomerism
rows.correct: Position isomers have the same skeleton and functional group but differ in the position of a substituent, multiple bond or functional group.
wrong: Position isomers have different molecular formulae.
rows.explanation: Position isomers have the same skeleton and functional group but differ in the position of a substituent, multiple bond or functional group.

rows.label: functional isomerism
rows.correct: Functional isomers share a molecular formula but contain different functional groups.
wrong: Functional isomers must belong to the same homologous series.
rows.explanation: Functional isomers share a molecular formula but contain different functional groups.

rows.label: stereoisomerism
rows.correct: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms.
wrong: Stereoisomers always have different connectivities.
rows.explanation: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms.

rows.label: homolytic fission
rows.correct: Homolytic cleavage gives one bonding electron to each fragment and forms free radicals.
wrong: Homolysis produces a carbocation and a carbanion.
rows.explanation: Homolytic cleavage gives one bonding electron to each fragment and forms free radicals.

rows.label: heterolytic fission
rows.correct: Heterolytic cleavage gives both bonding electrons to one fragment and forms ions.
wrong: Heterolysis always produces two free radicals.
rows.explanation: Heterolytic cleavage gives both bonding electrons to one fragment and forms ions.

rows.label: electrophiles and nucleophiles
rows.correct: An electrophile accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile donates an electron pair.
wrong: A nucleophile is necessarily positively charged.
rows.explanation: An electrophile accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile donates an electron pair.

rows.label: intermediate stability
rows.correct: Alkyl substitution generally stabilises simple carbocations and radicals but destabilises simple carbanions; resonance can dominate these trends.
wrong: Tertiary carbanions are always the most stable simple alkyl carbanions.
rows.explanation: Alkyl substitution generally stabilises simple carbocations and radicals but destabilises simple carbanions; resonance can dominate these trends.

rows.label: inductive effect
rows.correct: The inductive effect is permanent polarisation transmitted through sigma bonds and decreases rapidly with distance.
wrong: The inductive effect is transmitted without attenuation through a long chain.
rows.explanation: The inductive effect is permanent polarisation transmitted through sigma bonds and decreases rapidly with distance.

rows.label: resonance effect
rows.correct: Resonance delocalises pi or lone-pair electrons over a conjugated framework; the real species is a resonance hybrid.
wrong: Canonical forms are isolable molecules in rapid equilibrium.
rows.explanation: Resonance delocalises pi or lone-pair electrons over a conjugated framework; the real species is a resonance hybrid.

rows.label: electromeric effect
rows.correct: The electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of pi electrons under attack by a reagent.
wrong: The electromeric effect persists after the attacking reagent is removed.
rows.explanation: The electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of pi electrons under attack by a reagent.

rows.label: hyperconjugation
rows.correct: Hyperconjugation delocalises sigma electrons of an alpha C-H bond into an adjacent empty or pi orbital.
wrong: Hyperconjugation requires a lone pair on the alpha carbon.
rows.explanation: Hyperconjugation delocalises sigma electrons of an alpha C-H bond into an adjacent empty or pi orbital.

rows.label: substitution reaction
rows.correct: In substitution, one atom or group is replaced by another without necessarily changing the carbon skeleton.
wrong: Substitution always increases the number of pi bonds.
rows.explanation: In substitution, one atom or group is replaced by another without necessarily changing the carbon skeleton.

rows.label: addition reaction
rows.correct: Addition joins atoms or groups across a multiple bond and usually decreases pi-bond count.
wrong: Addition removes two groups to create a multiple bond.
rows.explanation: Addition joins atoms or groups across a multiple bond and usually decreases pi-bond count.

rows.label: elimination reaction
rows.correct: Elimination removes atoms or groups from adjacent atoms and commonly forms a multiple bond.
wrong: Elimination is identical to addition.
rows.explanation: Elimination removes atoms or groups from adjacent atoms and commonly forms a multiple bond.

rows.label: rearrangement reaction
rows.correct: A rearrangement changes connectivity within the reacting skeleton to form an isomeric intermediate or product.
wrong: A rearrangement cannot move a hydride or alkyl group.
rows.explanation: A rearrangement changes connectivity within the reacting skeleton to form an isomeric intermediate or product.

rows.label: crystallisation
rows.correct: Crystallisation uses solubility differences, ideally high solubility in hot solvent and low solubility in cold solvent.
wrong: A good crystallisation solvent dissolves the solid equally at all temperatures.
rows.explanation: Crystallisation uses solubility differences, ideally high solubility in hot solvent and low solubility in cold solvent.

rows.label: distillation and sublimation
rows.correct: Distillation separates volatile components using boiling behaviour; sublimation suits a sublimable solid mixed with non-sublimable impurities.
wrong: Sublimation is the preferred method for two miscible liquids.
rows.explanation: Distillation separates volatile components using boiling behaviour; sublimation suits a sublimable solid mixed with non-sublimable impurities.

rows.label: differential extraction
rows.correct: Differential extraction transfers a solute into an immiscible solvent in which it is more soluble; repeated small extractions are efficient.
wrong: The two extraction solvents should be completely miscible.
rows.explanation: Differential extraction transfers a solute into an immiscible solvent in which it is more soluble; repeated small extractions are efficient.

rows.label: chromatography
rows.correct: Chromatography separates components by different distributions between stationary and mobile phases.
wrong: All components must have identical affinities for both phases.
rows.explanation: Chromatography separates components by different distributions between stationary and mobile phases.

rows.label: carbon and hydrogen detection
rows.correct: On oxidation, carbon and hydrogen are detected through formation of CO2 and H2O using their characteristic tests.
wrong: Heating an organic compound always proves nitrogen is present.
rows.explanation: On oxidation, carbon and hydrogen are detected through formation of CO2 and H2O using their characteristic tests.

rows.label: Lassaigne sodium fusion
rows.correct: Sodium fusion converts covalently bound nitrogen, sulphur and halogens into water-soluble ionic salts.
wrong: Sodium fusion is used to volatilise all heteroatoms unchanged.
rows.explanation: Sodium fusion converts covalently bound nitrogen, sulphur and halogens into water-soluble ionic salts.

rows.label: nitrogen and sulphur tests
rows.correct: Nitrogen can be detected through Prussian blue chemistry; sulphur through characteristic sulphide reactions.
wrong: A positive halogen test directly proves nitrogen.
rows.explanation: Nitrogen can be detected through Prussian blue chemistry; sulphur through characteristic sulphide reactions.

rows.label: halogen test
rows.correct: After acidifying the sodium extract appropriately, AgCl is white, AgBr pale yellow and AgI yellow with different ammonia solubilities.
wrong: AgI is white and freely soluble in dilute ammonia.
rows.explanation: After acidifying the sodium extract appropriately, AgCl is white, AgBr pale yellow and AgI yellow with different ammonia solubilities.

rows.label: carbon-hydrogen estimation
rows.correct: Carbon and hydrogen percentages follow from measured CO2 and H2O masses using the carbon and hydrogen mass fractions in those products.
wrong: The mass of CO2 equals the mass of carbon in the sample.
rows.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen percentages follow from measured CO2 and H2O masses using the carbon and hydrogen mass fractions in those products.

rows.label: nitrogen estimation
rows.correct: Dumas and Kjeldahl methods estimate nitrogen by different measured products; method conditions and excluded nitrogen forms must be respected.
wrong: Kjeldahl estimation applies without limitation to every nitrogen compound.
rows.explanation: Dumas and Kjeldahl methods estimate nitrogen by different measured products; method conditions and excluded nitrogen forms must be respected.

rows.label: halogen and sulphur estimation
rows.correct: Carius analysis converts halogen or sulphur to a weighable silver halide or barium sulphate derivative.
wrong: Carius analysis estimates halogen from the mass of elemental halogen collected.
rows.explanation: Carius analysis converts halogen or sulphur to a weighable silver halide or barium sulphate derivative.

rows.label: percentage-to-formula calculation
rows.correct: Element percentages are converted to mole ratios, reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio, then scaled by molar mass when molecular formula is required.
wrong: Empirical formula is obtained directly by using percentage values as subscripts.
rows.explanation: Element percentages are converted to mole ratios, reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio, then scaled by molar mass when molecular formula is required.

rows.label: saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
rows.correct: Alkanes contain only carbon-carbon single bonds; alkenes and alkynes contain carbon-carbon multiple bonds.
wrong: A saturated hydrocarbon must contain a benzene ring.
rows.explanation: Alkanes contain only carbon-carbon single bonds; alkenes and alkynes contain carbon-carbon multiple bonds.

rows.label: aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons
rows.correct: Aliphatic hydrocarbons may be open-chain or non-aromatic cyclic; aromatic hydrocarbons satisfy aromatic delocalisation criteria.
wrong: Every ring hydrocarbon is aromatic.
rows.explanation: Aliphatic hydrocarbons may be open-chain or non-aromatic cyclic; aromatic hydrocarbons satisfy aromatic delocalisation criteria.

rows.label: hydrocarbon nomenclature
rows.correct: The parent chain includes the maximum number of multiple bonds and is numbered to give them the lowest locants before substituent tie-breaks.
wrong: The longest single-bond path always overrides multiple-bond inclusion.
rows.explanation: The parent chain includes the maximum number of multiple bonds and is numbered to give them the lowest locants before substituent tie-breaks.

rows.label: alkane chain isomerism
rows.correct: The number of chain isomers grows as the carbon skeleton can branch in constitutionally distinct ways.
wrong: Different conformations of one alkane are chain isomers.
rows.explanation: The number of chain isomers grows as the carbon skeleton can branch in constitutionally distinct ways.

rows.label: hydrogenation and reduction to alkanes
rows.correct: Catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes or alkynes and suitable reduction of alkyl halides can produce alkanes.
wrong: Hydrogenation of an alkene produces an alkyne.
rows.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes or alkynes and suitable reduction of alkyl halides can produce alkanes.

rows.label: Wurtz reaction
rows.correct: Wurtz coupling of alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether is most useful for symmetrical alkanes with even carbon counts.
wrong: Wurtz reaction gives a single pure unsymmetrical alkane from two different halides.
rows.explanation: Wurtz coupling of alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether is most useful for symmetrical alkanes with even carbon counts.

rows.label: decarboxylation and Kolbe electrolysis
rows.correct: Soda-lime decarboxylation shortens the carbon chain by one, whereas Kolbe electrolysis couples radicals from carboxylate ions.
wrong: Both methods necessarily preserve the carbon count of the starting acid.
rows.explanation: Soda-lime decarboxylation shortens the carbon chain by one, whereas Kolbe electrolysis couples radicals from carboxylate ions.

rows.label: alkane physical trends
rows.correct: Boiling point generally rises with molar mass and falls with branching among isomers because surface contact changes.
wrong: More branching always raises boiling point among isomeric alkanes.
rows.explanation: Boiling point generally rises with molar mass and falls with branching among isomers because surface contact changes.

rows.label: free-radical halogenation
rows.correct: Alkane halogenation proceeds through initiation, propagation and termination radical steps under light or heat.
wrong: The propagation stage consumes radicals without regenerating any radical.
rows.explanation: Alkane halogenation proceeds through initiation, propagation and termination radical steps under light or heat.

rows.label: halogenation selectivity
rows.correct: Bromination is slower but more selective than chlorination; product ratios depend on hydrogen type and reactivity.
wrong: All hydrogens in every alkane react at identical rates.
rows.explanation: Bromination is slower but more selective than chlorination; product ratios depend on hydrogen type and reactivity.

rows.label: combustion and controlled oxidation
rows.correct: Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O, while limited oxygen or catalysts can give incomplete or controlled oxidation products.
wrong: Incomplete combustion always gives only CO2 and H2O.
rows.explanation: Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O, while limited oxygen or catalysts can give incomplete or controlled oxidation products.

rows.label: ethane conformations
rows.correct: Staggered ethane is more stable than eclipsed ethane because torsional strain is lower; rotation interconverts conformations.
wrong: Eclipsed and staggered ethane are constitutional isomers.
rows.explanation: Staggered ethane is more stable than eclipsed ethane because torsional strain is lower; rotation interconverts conformations.

rows.label: alkene bonding
rows.correct: Each alkene carbon is usually sp2 hybridised; the double bond has one sigma and one pi bond and restricts free rotation.
wrong: A carbon-carbon double bond contains two sigma bonds.
rows.explanation: Each alkene carbon is usually sp2 hybridised; the double bond has one sigma and one pi bond and restricts free rotation.

rows.label: alkene geometrical isomerism
rows.correct: Geometrical isomerism requires each double-bond carbon to carry two different substituents.
wrong: Propene shows cis-trans isomerism because it contains a double bond.
rows.explanation: Geometrical isomerism requires each double-bond carbon to carry two different substituents.

rows.label: dehydrohalogenation
rows.correct: Alcoholic base can eliminate HX from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide to form an alkene.
wrong: Aqueous hydroxide always favours elimination over substitution.
rows.explanation: Alcoholic base can eliminate HX from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide to form an alkene.

rows.label: dehydration and dehalogenation
rows.correct: Dehydration of alcohols and dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides are standard routes to alkenes.
wrong: Dehydration adds water across a carbon-carbon bond.
rows.explanation: Dehydration of alcohols and dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides are standard routes to alkenes.

rows.label: electrophilic addition
rows.correct: An alkene pi bond attacks an electrophile, commonly forming a carbocation whose stability helps control the major product.
wrong: The first step of normal HX addition is nucleophilic attack by halide on a saturated carbon.
rows.explanation: An alkene pi bond attacks an electrophile, commonly forming a carbocation whose stability helps control the major product.

rows.label: Markovnikov and peroxide effects
rows.correct: Normal HX addition usually follows Markovnikov orientation; the peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition specifically with HBr.
wrong: Peroxide reverses the orientation of HCl, HBr and HI equally.
rows.explanation: Normal HX addition usually follows Markovnikov orientation; the peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition specifically with HBr.

rows.label: alkene oxidation
rows.correct: Cold dilute alkaline permanganate gives vicinal diols, while stronger oxidative conditions can cleave the double bond.
wrong: Mild permanganate oxidation leaves the carbon-carbon double bond unchanged.
rows.explanation: Cold dilute alkaline permanganate gives vicinal diols, while stronger oxidative conditions can cleave the double bond.

rows.label: ozonolysis
rows.correct: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond and converts each alkene carbon into a carbonyl carbon.
wrong: Ozonolysis preserves the carbon-carbon double bond in both products.
rows.explanation: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond and converts each alkene carbon into a carbonyl carbon.

rows.label: alkyne structure
rows.correct: Triple-bonded carbons are sp hybridised and linear; a triple bond contains one sigma and two mutually perpendicular pi bonds.
wrong: A carbon-carbon triple bond contains three sigma bonds.
rows.explanation: Triple-bonded carbons are sp hybridised and linear; a triple bond contains one sigma and two mutually perpendicular pi bonds.

rows.label: terminal alkyne acidity
rows.correct: Terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes and alkanes because the conjugate base places charge in an orbital with greater s character.
wrong: All internal alkynes contain an acidic acetylenic hydrogen.
rows.explanation: Terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes and alkanes because the conjugate base places charge in an orbital with greater s character.

rows.label: alkyne preparation
rows.correct: Double dehydrohalogenation of suitable dihalides and hydrolysis of calcium carbide are standard alkyne preparations.
wrong: Single dehydrohalogenation of a monohalide directly forms an alkyne in one step.
rows.explanation: Double dehydrohalogenation of suitable dihalides and hydrolysis of calcium carbide are standard alkyne preparations.

rows.label: alkyne addition and polymerisation
rows.correct: Alkynes undergo stepwise addition; hydration gives an enol that tautomerises to a carbonyl compound, and ethyne can trimerise to benzene.
wrong: Hydration of an alkyne stops permanently at a stable isolated enol.
rows.explanation: Alkynes undergo stepwise addition; hydration gives an enol that tautomerises to a carbonyl compound, and ethyne can trimerise to benzene.

rows.label: benzene structure
rows.correct: Benzene is planar with six equivalent carbon-carbon bonds and delocalised pi electrons.
wrong: Benzene has three short double bonds alternating with three long single bonds.
rows.explanation: Benzene is planar with six equivalent carbon-carbon bonds and delocalised pi electrons.

rows.label: aromaticity
rows.correct: A cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system is aromatic when it contains 4n+2 pi electrons.
wrong: Every planar ring with 4n pi electrons is aromatic.
rows.explanation: A cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system is aromatic when it contains 4n+2 pi electrons.

rows.label: benzene stability
rows.correct: Resonance delocalisation makes benzene more stable than a hypothetical localised cyclohexatriene and favours substitution over addition.
wrong: Benzene readily undergoes addition because its pi bonds behave as three isolated alkenes.
rows.explanation: Resonance delocalisation makes benzene more stable than a hypothetical localised cyclohexatriene and favours substitution over addition.

rows.label: benzene preparation
rows.correct: Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate, reduction of phenol, and trimerisation of ethyne are NCERT routes to benzene.
wrong: Soda-lime decarboxylation of sodium benzoate gives toluene.
rows.explanation: Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate, reduction of phenol, and trimerisation of ethyne are NCERT routes to benzene.

rows.label: electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism
rows.correct: The ring attacks an electrophile, forms a sigma complex, then loses H+ to restore aromaticity.
wrong: The final step permanently destroys aromaticity.
rows.explanation: The ring attacks an electrophile, forms a sigma complex, then loses H+ to restore aromaticity.

rows.label: nitration and halogenation
rows.correct: Nitration generates NO2+ from concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids; halogenation uses a Lewis-acid catalyst to activate the halogen.
wrong: Benzene nitration uses hydroxide ion as the electrophile.
rows.explanation: Nitration generates NO2+ from concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids; halogenation uses a Lewis-acid catalyst to activate the halogen.

rows.label: Friedel-Crafts reactions
rows.correct: Friedel-Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group and acylation introduces an acyl group using Lewis-acid catalysis, subject to known limitations.
wrong: Friedel-Crafts acylation initially installs only an alkyl group with no carbonyl.
rows.explanation: Friedel-Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group and acylation introduces an acyl group using Lewis-acid catalysis, subject to known limitations.

rows.label: directing effects
rows.correct: Electron-donating groups generally activate and direct ortho/para; strong electron-withdrawing groups generally deactivate and direct meta, with halogens deactivating yet ortho/para directing.
wrong: Every deactivating group is meta directing without exception.
rows.explanation: Electron-donating groups generally activate and direct ortho/para; strong electron-withdrawing groups generally deactivate and direct meta, with halogens deactivating yet ortho/para directing.

rows.label: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon risk
rows.correct: Several fused-ring aromatic hydrocarbons formed during incomplete combustion are carcinogenic and must be handled as hazardous substances.
wrong: All hydrocarbons have identical toxicity and carcinogenicity.
rows.explanation: Several fused-ring aromatic hydrocarbons formed during incomplete combustion are carcinogenic and must be handled as hazardous substances.

rows.label: safe interpretation of toxicity
rows.correct: Toxicity depends on chemical identity, dose and exposure; an NCERT hazard statement should not be generalised to every hydrocarbon.
wrong: A natural source makes an aromatic hydrocarbon automatically harmless.
rows.explanation: Toxicity depends on chemical identity, dose and exposure; an NCERT hazard statement should not be generalised to every hydrocarbon.

rows.label: Molarity
rows.correct: moles of solute per litre of solution
rows.explanation: Molarity changes with temperature because solution volume changes.

rows.label: Molality
rows.correct: moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
rows.explanation: Molality is independent of temperature because it uses mass of solvent.

rows.label: Mole fraction
rows.correct: moles of one component divided by total moles of all components
rows.explanation: The sum of mole fractions in a solution is one.

rows.label: Raoult law
rows.correct: partial vapour pressure equals mole fraction multiplied by vapour pressure of the pure component
rows.explanation: It describes ideal-solution vapour pressure.

rows.label: Ideal solution
rows.correct: obeys Raoult law over the entire composition range
rows.explanation: For an ideal solution, enthalpy and volume of mixing are zero.

rows.label: Positive deviation
rows.correct: vapour pressure is greater than predicted by Raoult law
rows.explanation: Weaker unlike interactions favour escape to vapour and may form a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

rows.label: Negative deviation
rows.correct: vapour pressure is less than predicted by Raoult law
rows.explanation: Stronger unlike interactions may produce a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

rows.label: Henry law
rows.correct: gas solubility is related to its partial pressure by p equals KH times mole fraction
rows.explanation: At a given pressure, a larger Henry constant means lower solubility.

rows.label: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
rows.correct: equals solute mole fraction for a dilute solution of nonvolatile solute
rows.explanation: It is a colligative property.

rows.label: Elevation of boiling point
rows.correct: delta Tb equals Kb times molality
rows.explanation: A nonvolatile solute raises the boiling point of a solvent.

rows.label: Depression of freezing point
rows.correct: delta Tf equals Kf times molality
rows.explanation: A solute lowers the freezing point of a solvent.

rows.label: Osmotic pressure
rows.correct: pi equals concentration times R times T for a dilute solution
rows.explanation: Osmotic pressure is useful for molar-mass determination of biomolecules.

rows.label: Reverse osmosis
rows.correct: solvent is forced through a semipermeable membrane by pressure exceeding osmotic pressure
rows.explanation: It is used in desalination and water purification.

rows.label: van't Hoff factor
rows.correct: ratio of observed to calculated colligative property
rows.explanation: Dissociation usually gives i greater than one and association gives i less than one.

rows.label: Isotonic solutions
rows.correct: have the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature
rows.explanation: There is no net osmosis between isotonic solutions through a semipermeable membrane.

rows.label: Azeotrope
rows.correct: mixture that boils at constant composition
rows.explanation: Its liquid and vapour phases have the same composition.

rows.label: Conductance
rows.correct: reciprocal of resistance
rows.explanation: Conductance is measured in siemens.

rows.label: Conductivity
rows.correct: conductance of a solution column of unit length and unit cross-sectional area
rows.explanation: Conductivity decreases on dilution because ions per unit volume decrease.

rows.label: Molar conductivity
rows.correct: conductivity multiplied by volume containing one mole of electrolyte
rows.explanation: Molar conductivity generally increases on dilution.

rows.label: Kohlrausch law
rows.correct: limiting molar conductivity is the sum of limiting ionic contributions
rows.explanation: It helps calculate limiting conductivity of weak electrolytes.

rows.label: Galvanic cell
rows.correct: converts spontaneous chemical energy into electrical energy
rows.explanation: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

rows.label: Cell notation
rows.correct: anode is written on the left and cathode on the right
rows.explanation: A double vertical line denotes the salt bridge.

rows.label: Standard cell potential
rows.correct: standard cathode reduction potential minus standard anode reduction potential
rows.explanation: A positive value corresponds to a spontaneous cell reaction under standard conditions.

rows.label: Nernst equation
rows.correct: E equals E standard minus RT over nF times natural log Q
rows.explanation: Cell potential depends on concentration and temperature.

rows.label: Gibbs energy and cell potential
rows.correct: delta G equals minus nFE
rows.explanation: A positive cell potential gives negative Gibbs energy.

rows.label: Equilibrium constant and cell potential
rows.correct: standard cell potential equals RT over nF times natural log K
rows.explanation: A larger positive standard potential corresponds to a larger equilibrium constant.

rows.label: Salt bridge
rows.correct: maintains electrical neutrality and completes the circuit
