rows.explanation: It minimises liquid-junction potential without mixing the bulk solutions rapidly.

rows.label: Electrolytic cell
rows.correct: uses external electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous reaction
rows.explanation: The anode remains the site of oxidation.

rows.label: Faraday first law
rows.correct: mass deposited is proportional to quantity of electricity passed
rows.explanation: Charge equals current multiplied by time.

rows.label: Faraday constant
rows.correct: charge carried by one mole of electrons
rows.explanation: Its value is approximately 96500 coulomb per mole.

rows.label: Corrosion of iron
rows.correct: electrochemical oxidation produces hydrated iron(III) oxide
rows.explanation: Moisture and oxygen are required for ordinary rusting.

rows.label: Fuel cell
rows.correct: converts continuously supplied fuel and oxidant directly into electrical energy
rows.explanation: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells produce water as the main product.

rows.label: Average reaction rate
rows.correct: change in concentration divided by the corresponding time interval
rows.explanation: Stoichiometric coefficients are used to express one common reaction rate.

rows.label: Instantaneous rate
rows.correct: slope of the concentration-time tangent at a specified instant
rows.explanation: It is the limiting value of average rate as the interval approaches zero.

rows.label: Rate law
rows.correct: rate equals k times reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers
rows.explanation: Rate-law exponents need not equal stoichiometric coefficients.

rows.label: Order of reaction
rows.correct: sum of powers of concentration terms in the rate law
rows.explanation: Order is determined experimentally.

rows.label: Molecularity
rows.correct: number of reacting species in an elementary step
rows.explanation: Molecularity is a positive integer and is not defined for an overall complex reaction.

rows.label: Zero-order reaction
rows.correct: rate is independent of reactant concentration
rows.explanation: Its concentration-time graph is linear with slope minus k.

rows.label: Zero-order half-life
rows.correct: t half equals initial concentration divided by two k
rows.explanation: Its half-life depends on initial concentration.

rows.label: First-order reaction
rows.correct: log initial concentration over final concentration equals kt over 2.303
rows.explanation: Its rate constant has unit time inverse.

rows.label: First-order half-life
rows.correct: t half equals 0.693 over k
rows.explanation: It is independent of initial concentration.

rows.label: Pseudo-first-order reaction
rows.correct: one reactant is present in large excess so its concentration is effectively constant
rows.explanation: Hydrolysis with water in large excess is a common example.

rows.label: Arrhenius equation
rows.correct: k equals A e raised to minus Ea over RT
rows.explanation: Increasing temperature raises the fraction of molecules crossing the activation barrier.

rows.label: Activation energy
rows.correct: minimum energy barrier associated with reaction progress
rows.explanation: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy.

rows.label: Catalyst and equilibrium
rows.correct: a catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally
rows.explanation: It does not change equilibrium constant or equilibrium composition.

rows.label: Collision frequency
rows.correct: number of molecular collisions per unit time and volume
rows.explanation: Only collisions with sufficient energy and proper orientation are effective.

rows.label: Temperature coefficient
rows.correct: reaction rate commonly increases when temperature rises
rows.explanation: The increase arises mainly from the larger high-energy fraction.

rows.label: Rate-determining step
rows.correct: slowest elementary step controlling the overall rate
rows.explanation: A proposed mechanism must agree with the observed rate law.

rows.label: Transition element
rows.correct: element whose atom or common ion has an incompletely filled d subshell
rows.explanation: Zinc is not a transition element because Zn and Zn2+ have filled d subshells.

rows.label: General d-block configuration
rows.correct: is (n minus 1)d one to ten ns zero to two
rows.explanation: Chromium and copper show stability-related configuration exceptions.

rows.label: Variable oxidation states
rows.correct: arise because ns and (n minus 1)d electrons have comparable energies
rows.explanation: Middle-series elements commonly show several oxidation states.

rows.label: Coloured ions
rows.correct: often result from d-d electronic transitions
rows.explanation: Ions with d zero or d ten configurations are generally colourless.

rows.label: Paramagnetism
rows.correct: arises from unpaired electrons
rows.explanation: Spin-only magnetic moment is root of n into n plus two Bohr magnetons.

rows.label: Catalytic activity
rows.correct: is favoured by variable oxidation states and surface adsorption
rows.explanation: Transition metals and their compounds often act as catalysts.

rows.label: Complex formation
rows.correct: is promoted by small ionic size, high charge and available orbitals
rows.explanation: Transition-metal ions readily bind ligands.

rows.label: Interstitial compounds
rows.correct: form when small atoms occupy holes in a metal lattice
rows.explanation: They are often hard and retain metallic conductivity.

rows.label: Alloy formation
rows.correct: is favoured by similar atomic radii of transition metals
rows.explanation: Substitution in metallic lattices gives solid solutions.

rows.label: Lanthanoid contraction
rows.correct: steady decrease in lanthanoid ionic radii across the series
rows.explanation: Poor shielding by 4f electrons causes the contraction.

rows.label: Zirconium-hafnium similarity
rows.correct: results from lanthanoid contraction
rows.explanation: Their radii are nearly equal and separation is difficult.

rows.label: Lanthanoid oxidation state
rows.correct: plus three is the most common state
rows.explanation: Plus two and plus four occur when they give especially stable f configurations.

rows.label: Actinoid oxidation states
rows.correct: show wider variability than lanthanoids
rows.explanation: 5f, 6d and 7s levels have comparable energies.

rows.label: Potassium permanganate
rows.correct: is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium
rows.explanation: Permanganate is reduced mainly to Mn2+ in acid.

rows.label: Potassium dichromate
rows.correct: is an orange oxidising agent in acidic medium
rows.explanation: Dichromate is reduced to green Cr3+.

rows.label: Chromate-dichromate equilibrium
rows.correct: acid favours orange dichromate and base favours yellow chromate
rows.explanation: The interconversion depends on hydrogen-ion concentration.

rows.label: Coordination entity
rows.correct: central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ligands
rows.explanation: The species inside square brackets is treated as one entity.

rows.label: Ligand
rows.correct: Lewis base that donates an electron pair to a metal centre
rows.explanation: Ligands may be neutral, anionic or cationic.

rows.label: Coordination number
rows.correct: number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal
rows.explanation: A bidentate ligand contributes two to coordination number.

rows.label: Denticity
rows.correct: number of donor atoms through which one ligand binds
rows.explanation: EDTA is hexadentate.

rows.label: Chelation
rows.correct: ring formation by a multidentate ligand attached to one metal
rows.explanation: Chelates are commonly more stable than analogous monodentate complexes.

rows.label: Oxidation number in a complex
rows.correct: is found by balancing ligand charges with the complex charge
rows.explanation: Neutral ligands do not contribute ionic charge.

rows.label: Werner theory
rows.correct: distinguishes primary valency from secondary valency
rows.explanation: Secondary valency corresponds to coordination number and is directional.

rows.label: Ionisation isomerism
rows.correct: exchange occurs between a coordinated ion and a counter ion
rows.explanation: The isomers give different ions in solution.

rows.label: Linkage isomerism
rows.correct: an ambidentate ligand coordinates through different donor atoms
rows.explanation: Nitrite can bind through nitrogen or oxygen.

rows.label: Geometrical isomerism
rows.correct: arises from different spatial arrangements such as cis and trans
rows.explanation: Square-planar and octahedral complexes commonly show it.

rows.label: Optical isomerism
rows.correct: non-superimposable mirror-image complexes rotate plane-polarised light oppositely
rows.explanation: Some chelate complexes are optically active.

rows.label: Crystal-field splitting
rows.correct: ligand approach removes degeneracy of metal d orbitals
rows.explanation: Octahedral splitting gives lower t2g and higher eg sets.

rows.label: Strong-field ligand
rows.correct: can produce a large splitting and electron pairing
rows.explanation: Cyanide is stronger-field than fluoride in the spectrochemical series.

rows.label: High-spin complex
rows.correct: contains the maximum number of unpaired electrons allowed by a small splitting
rows.explanation: Weak-field ligands favour high spin.

rows.label: Coordination-compound colour
rows.correct: often arises from absorption associated with d-orbital transitions
rows.explanation: Observed colour is complementary to absorbed light.

rows.label: IUPAC complex naming
rows.correct: ligands are named before the metal and anionic metal complexes use an ate ending
rows.explanation: Oxidation state of the metal is written in Roman numerals.

rows.label: Carbon-halogen bond polarity
rows.correct: carbon bears partial positive charge and halogen partial negative charge
rows.explanation: Bond polarity makes the carbon susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

rows.label: SN2 reaction
rows.correct: concerted backside attack gives inversion of configuration
rows.explanation: Its rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile concentration.

rows.label: SN1 reaction
rows.correct: proceeds through a planar carbocation intermediate
rows.explanation: Its rate depends mainly on substrate concentration.

rows.label: SN1 substrate preference
rows.correct: tertiary halides react faster because their carbocations are more stable
rows.explanation: Polar protic solvents support ionisation.

rows.label: SN2 substrate preference
rows.correct: methyl and primary halides react faster because steric hindrance is low
rows.explanation: Tertiary halides are strongly hindered for backside attack.

rows.label: Walden inversion
rows.correct: configuration is inverted in an SN2 displacement
rows.explanation: Backside attack reverses the tetrahedral arrangement.

rows.label: Elimination reaction
rows.correct: alcoholic base can remove hydrogen halide to form an alkene
rows.explanation: More substituted alkene is commonly the major Saytzeff product.

rows.label: Finkelstein reaction
rows.correct: alkyl chloride or bromide is converted to alkyl iodide using sodium iodide in acetone
rows.explanation: Precipitation of sodium chloride or bromide drives the reaction.

rows.label: Swarts reaction
rows.correct: alkyl chloride or bromide is converted to alkyl fluoride using a metal fluoride
rows.explanation: It is used to prepare fluoroalkanes.

rows.label: Wurtz reaction
rows.correct: alkyl halides couple with sodium in dry ether
rows.explanation: Symmetrical higher alkanes are obtained most cleanly.

rows.label: Aryl carbon-halogen bond
rows.correct: has partial double-bond character because of resonance
rows.explanation: Chlorobenzene is less reactive than chloroethane toward nucleophilic substitution.

rows.label: Haloarene carbon hybridisation
rows.correct: halogen is bonded to an sp2 carbon
rows.explanation: The shorter stronger bond resists cleavage.

rows.label: Grignard reagent
rows.correct: organomagnesium halide is strongly nucleophilic and basic
rows.explanation: It must be prepared under anhydrous conditions.

rows.label: Chirality
rows.correct: a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups may be stereogenic
rows.explanation: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions.

rows.label: DDT persistence
rows.correct: arises from resistance to biodegradation
rows.explanation: Its biomagnification causes environmental concern.

rows.label: Freon impact
rows.correct: chlorofluorocarbons release radicals that destroy stratospheric ozone
rows.explanation: Their chemical stability lets them reach the stratosphere.

rows.label: Alcohol classification
rows.correct: primary, secondary and tertiary labels depend on substitution at the carbon bearing hydroxyl
rows.explanation: This classification predicts oxidation and substitution behaviour.

rows.label: Alcohol boiling point
rows.correct: is high relative to similar hydrocarbons because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding
rows.explanation: Boiling point generally rises with molecular mass and falls with branching.

rows.label: Alcohol acidity
rows.correct: alcohols are weaker acids than water in many alkyl cases
rows.explanation: Electron-releasing alkyl groups destabilise alkoxide ions.

rows.label: Lucas test
rows.correct: tertiary alcohol gives immediate turbidity with concentrated HCl and zinc chloride
rows.explanation: Turbidity is due to insoluble alkyl chloride formation.

rows.label: Alcohol dehydration
rows.correct: concentrated acid and heat convert alcohol to alkene
rows.explanation: More substituted alkene is commonly favoured.

rows.label: Primary alcohol oxidation
rows.correct: can give aldehyde and then carboxylic acid
rows.explanation: Controlled oxidation is needed to stop at aldehyde.

rows.label: Secondary alcohol oxidation
rows.correct: gives a ketone
rows.explanation: Further oxidation requires carbon-carbon bond cleavage.

rows.label: Tertiary alcohol oxidation
rows.correct: does not occur readily without carbon-carbon bond cleavage
rows.explanation: There is no hydrogen on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon.

rows.label: Phenol acidity
rows.correct: phenol is more acidic than alcohol because phenoxide is resonance-stabilised
rows.explanation: Electron-withdrawing ring groups increase phenol acidity.

rows.label: Kolbe reaction
rows.correct: sodium phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide then acidification gives salicylic acid
rows.explanation: Carboxylation occurs mainly at the ortho position.

rows.label: Reimer-Tiemann reaction
rows.correct: phenol with chloroform and base gives salicylaldehyde after work-up
rows.explanation: The formyl group enters mainly at the ortho position.

rows.label: Williamson synthesis
rows.correct: alkoxide reacts with primary alkyl halide by SN2 to form ether
rows.explanation: Tertiary halide favours elimination rather than ether formation.

rows.label: Ether cleavage
rows.correct: hot concentrated hydrogen iodide cleaves carbon-oxygen bonds
rows.explanation: In aryl alkyl ether, cleavage occurs at the alkyl oxygen bond.

rows.label: Anisole substitution
rows.correct: methoxy group activates the ring and directs ortho and para
rows.explanation: Resonance donation increases ring electron density.

rows.label: Hydrogen bonding and solubility
rows.correct: lower alcohols mix well with water through hydrogen bonding
rows.explanation: Solubility decreases as the hydrophobic alkyl group grows.

rows.label: Alcohol with sodium
rows.correct: forms alkoxide and liberates hydrogen gas
rows.explanation: The reaction demonstrates cleavage of the oxygen-hydrogen bond.

rows.label: Carbonyl carbon
rows.correct: is electrophilic because the carbon-oxygen bond is polar
rows.explanation: Nucleophiles attack the carbonyl carbon.

rows.label: Nucleophilic addition
rows.correct: converts the trigonal carbonyl carbon toward a tetrahedral product
rows.explanation: Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones.

rows.label: Aldehyde reactivity
rows.correct: is greater than ketone reactivity because steric and electron-donating effects are smaller
rows.explanation: Formaldehyde is especially reactive.

rows.label: HCN addition
rows.correct: aldehyde or ketone forms a cyanohydrin
rows.explanation: The product contains hydroxyl and cyano groups on the former carbonyl carbon.

rows.label: Sodium bisulphite addition
rows.correct: many aldehydes and ketones form crystalline addition products
rows.explanation: The reaction can help purification and separation.

rows.label: Grignard addition
rows.correct: carbonyl compounds give alcohols after hydrolysis
rows.explanation: Formaldehyde gives primary, other aldehydes secondary and ketones tertiary alcohols.

rows.label: Tollens test
rows.correct: aldehyde reduces diamminesilver(I) to a silver mirror
rows.explanation: Most ketones do not respond.

rows.label: Fehling test
rows.correct: aliphatic aldehyde reduces copper(II) to brick-red copper(I) oxide
rows.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes generally do not give the test.

rows.label: Iodoform test
rows.correct: methyl ketones and compounds oxidisable to them give yellow triiodomethane
rows.explanation: Ethanol and secondary alcohols with a methyl group can respond.

rows.label: Aldol condensation
rows.correct: aldehyde or ketone with alpha hydrogen forms a beta-hydroxy carbonyl then may dehydrate
rows.explanation: Enolate formation initiates the reaction.

rows.label: Cannizzaro reaction
rows.correct: aldehyde without alpha hydrogen disproportionates in concentrated base
rows.explanation: One molecule is oxidised and another reduced.

rows.label: Clemmensen reduction
rows.correct: zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid reduce carbonyl to methylene
rows.explanation: It is performed in acidic medium.

rows.label: Wolff-Kishner reduction
rows.correct: hydrazine and strong base reduce carbonyl to methylene
rows.explanation: It is performed in strongly basic medium.

rows.label: Carboxylic acid acidity
rows.correct: carboxylate ion is stabilised by equivalent resonance structures
rows.explanation: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols and alcohols.

rows.label: Esterification
rows.correct: carboxylic acid and alcohol form ester in presence of acid
rows.explanation: The reversible reaction also forms water.

rows.label: Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction
rows.correct: carboxylic acid with alpha hydrogen undergoes alpha halogenation
rows.explanation: Halogen substitutes at the carbon adjacent to carboxyl.

rows.label: Amine basicity
rows.correct: lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton
rows.explanation: Availability of the lone pair controls basic strength.

rows.label: Aniline basicity
rows.correct: is lower than ammonia because the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring
rows.explanation: Electron-withdrawing substituents further reduce basicity.

rows.label: Amine classification
rows.correct: primary, secondary and tertiary labels count carbon groups attached to nitrogen
rows.explanation: Quaternary ammonium ion has four carbon substituents and positive charge.

rows.label: Gabriel synthesis
rows.correct: phthalimide route gives primary alkyl amines
rows.explanation: It is not suitable for preparing aryl amines.

rows.label: Hofmann bromamide reaction
rows.correct: amide gives a primary amine with one fewer carbon
rows.explanation: Bromine and strong base bring about rearrangement.

rows.label: Carbylamine test
rows.correct: primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic base gives foul-smelling isocyanide
rows.explanation: Secondary and tertiary amines do not give the test.

rows.label: Hinsberg test
rows.correct: benzenesulphonyl chloride distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary amines
rows.explanation: Solubility behaviour of sulphonamide products differs.

rows.label: Nitrous acid with primary aliphatic amine
rows.correct: gives unstable diazonium species that evolves nitrogen
rows.explanation: An alcohol is commonly formed.

rows.label: Diazotisation
rows.correct: primary aromatic amine forms diazonium salt at 273 to 278 kelvin
rows.explanation: Low temperature stabilises the diazonium salt.

rows.label: Diazonium substitution
rows.correct: diazonium group can be replaced by halogen, cyano or hydroxyl
rows.explanation: Diazonium chemistry introduces groups difficult to install directly.

rows.label: Sandmeyer reaction
rows.correct: copper(I) salts replace diazonium by chlorine, bromine or cyano
rows.explanation: Nitrogen gas is released.

rows.label: Azo coupling
rows.correct: diazonium ion couples with activated aromatic ring to form an azo compound
rows.explanation: Phenol and aniline give brightly coloured products.

rows.label: Aniline bromination
rows.correct: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline
rows.explanation: The amino group strongly activates ortho and para positions.

rows.label: Acylation of amine
rows.correct: reduces nitrogen basicity by delocalising the lone pair into carbonyl
rows.explanation: Acetanilide is less activating than aniline.

rows.label: Ammonolysis of alkyl halide
rows.correct: can produce a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines
rows.explanation: Further alkylation of the initially formed amine causes mixtures.

rows.label: Amide reduction
rows.correct: lithium aluminium hydride converts amide carbonyl to methylene
rows.explanation: The product is an amine with the same carbon skeleton.

rows.label: Monosaccharide
rows.correct: carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed to simpler carbohydrate
rows.explanation: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides.

rows.label: Glucose
rows.correct: aldohexose with six carbon atoms and an aldehyde function in open-chain form
rows.explanation: Its predominant solution forms are cyclic hemiacetals.

rows.label: Fructose
rows.correct: ketohexose with a ketone function in open-chain form
rows.explanation: It commonly forms a five-membered cyclic hemiketal.

rows.label: Anomers
rows.correct: cyclic sugar forms differing at the anomeric carbon
rows.explanation: Alpha and beta glucose interconvert through mutarotation.

rows.label: Sucrose
rows.correct: nonreducing disaccharide of glucose and fructose
rows.explanation: Both anomeric carbons participate in its glycosidic bond.

rows.label: Maltose
rows.correct: reducing disaccharide of two glucose units
rows.explanation: It contains an alpha one-to-four glycosidic linkage.

rows.label: Lactose
rows.correct: reducing disaccharide of galactose and glucose
rows.explanation: It contains a beta one-to-four glycosidic linkage.

rows.label: Starch
rows.correct: plant storage polysaccharide made of alpha glucose
rows.explanation: Amylose is mainly unbranched and amylopectin is branched.

rows.label: Cellulose
rows.correct: linear polymer of beta glucose
rows.explanation: Humans cannot digest its beta one-to-four links.

rows.label: Glycogen
rows.correct: highly branched animal storage polysaccharide
rows.explanation: It is stored mainly in liver and muscle.

rows.label: Amino acid zwitterion
rows.correct: contains both ammonium and carboxylate groups in one molecule
rows.explanation: At isoelectric point it has no net charge.

rows.label: Peptide bond
rows.correct: amide linkage formed between amino and carboxyl groups
rows.explanation: Protein hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds.

rows.label: Protein primary structure
rows.correct: specific sequence of amino acids
rows.explanation: Changing one residue can alter protein function.

rows.label: Protein denaturation
rows.correct: loss of secondary and tertiary structure without breaking primary peptide sequence
rows.explanation: Heat or pH can destroy biological activity.

rows.label: DNA sugar
rows.correct: two-deoxyribose
rows.explanation: DNA contains thymine and is usually double-stranded.

rows.label: RNA sugar
rows.correct: ribose
rows.explanation: RNA contains uracil and is commonly single-stranded.

chapters.name: p-Block Elements: Trends and First-Element Behaviour

rows.label: Group 13 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np¹
rows.explanation: There are three valence electrons in the general group 13 configuration.

rows.label: Group 14 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np²
rows.explanation: There are four valence electrons in the general group 14 configuration.

rows.label: Group 15 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np³
rows.explanation: There are five valence electrons in the general group 15 configuration.

rows.label: Group 16 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np⁴
rows.explanation: There are six valence electrons in the general group 16 configuration.

rows.label: Group 17 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np⁵
rows.explanation: There are seven valence electrons in the general group 17 configuration.

rows.label: Group 18 configuration except helium
rows.correct: ns²np⁶
rows.explanation: A filled valence shell is characteristic of noble gases other than helium.

rows.label: Helium configuration
rows.correct: 1s²
rows.explanation: The first shell is complete with two electrons.

rows.label: Atomic size down a p-block group
rows.correct: generally increases because additional electron shells are occupied
rows.explanation: Compare the same kind of atomic radius when making a trend.

rows.label: First ionisation enthalpy across a period
rows.correct: generally rises with effective nuclear charge, with configuration-related exceptions
rows.explanation: Subshell and pairing effects can produce local deviations.

rows.label: Electronegativity down a p-block group
rows.correct: generally decreases as atomic size and shielding increase
rows.explanation: This is a general trend rather than a rule without exceptions.

rows.label: Inert-pair effect
rows.correct: increasing reluctance of the outer ns² pair to participate in bonding in heavier elements
rows.explanation: It helps stabilise oxidation states two units below the group maximum.

rows.label: Group 13 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +1 becomes more stable toward the heavier members
rows.explanation: The inert-pair effect favours retention of the ns² pair.

rows.label: Group 14 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +2 is relatively more stable for heavier members than for lighter members
rows.explanation: Lead commonly shows a stable +2 state.

rows.label: Group 15 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +3 gains relative stability compared with +5 down the group
rows.explanation: This is associated with the inert-pair effect.

rows.label: Small size of the first p-block member
rows.correct: contributes to its anomalous behaviour relative to heavier congeners
rows.explanation: High charge density affects bonding and physical properties.

rows.label: Second-period octet restriction
rows.correct: second-period central atoms do not expand their valence octet
rows.explanation: Boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine lack an available third shell in the standard valence model.

rows.label: Carbon catenation
rows.correct: strong carbon-carbon bonds support extensive chains and rings
rows.explanation: Catenation is the ability to form bonds to atoms of the same element.

rows.label: Carbon versus silicon multiple bonding
rows.correct: carbon forms strong pπ-pπ multiple bonds more readily
rows.explanation: The compact second-period orbitals overlap more effectively.

rows.label: Nitrogen molecule
rows.correct: contains a strong N≡N triple bond
rows.explanation: This contributes to the low reactivity of nitrogen under ordinary conditions.

rows.label: Nitrogen versus phosphorus valence
rows.correct: nitrogen does not form a neutral pentahalide analogous to PCl₅ in the octet model
rows.explanation: Nitrogen cannot accommodate ten electrons in its second-shell valence region.

rows.label: Oxygen versus sulfur molecular form
rows.correct: oxygen commonly occurs as O₂ whereas sulfur commonly occurs as S₈
rows.explanation: Differences in bonding favour different elemental molecular structures.

rows.label: Fluorine oxidation state in compounds
rows.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and does not show positive oxidation states in its compounds.

rows.label: Halogen elemental molecules
rows.correct: diatomic X₂ molecules
rows.explanation: Group 17 elements occur in paired elemental molecules under usual molecular conditions.

rows.label: Chlorine versus fluorine electron gain enthalpy
rows.correct: chlorine has a more negative first electron gain enthalpy
rows.explanation: Small fluorine orbitals increase repulsion for an added electron.

rows.label: Noble-gas low ordinary reactivity
rows.correct: filled valence shells and high ionisation enthalpies
rows.explanation: Heavier members can form compounds under suitable conditions.

rows.label: Metallic character down p-block groups
rows.correct: generally increases
rows.explanation: Larger atoms tend to lose valence electrons more readily.

rows.label: Acidity of main-group oxides across a period
rows.correct: generally increases as nonmetallic character increases
rows.explanation: Metallic oxides tend to be basic whereas many nonmetal oxides are acidic.

rows.label: Boron bonding tendency
rows.correct: predominantly covalent compounds rather than simple B³⁺ salts
rows.explanation: The small atom and high ionisation requirements disfavour formation of a simple B³⁺ ion.

rows.label: Crystallisation
rows.correct: purifies a solid using different solubilities in hot and cold solvent
rows.explanation: The desired solid crystallises on cooling while many soluble impurities remain in solution.

rows.label: Simple distillation
rows.correct: separates a volatile liquid from nonvolatile impurities or liquids with widely separated boiling points
rows.explanation: Vapour is condensed to collect the volatile component.

rows.label: Fractional distillation
rows.correct: separates miscible liquids with relatively close boiling points
rows.explanation: A fractionating column provides repeated vapour-liquid equilibration.

rows.label: Steam distillation
rows.correct: isolates a steam-volatile substance immiscible with water
rows.explanation: The mixture can distil below the boiling point of the organic component alone.

rows.label: Sublimation
rows.correct: separates a sublimable solid from nonsublimable impurities
rows.explanation: The volatile solid passes through vapour and is deposited on cooling.

rows.label: Chromatography
rows.correct: separates components by different distribution between stationary and mobile phases
rows.explanation: Different affinities produce different migration speeds.

rows.label: Rf in planar chromatography
rows.correct: distance travelled by solute divided by distance travelled by solvent front
rows.explanation: Both distances are measured from the origin.

rows.label: Lassaigne sodium fusion
rows.correct: converts covalently bound heteroatoms into water-soluble ionic salts
rows.explanation: The extract can then be tested for nitrogen, sulfur and halogens.

rows.label: Nitrogen in Lassaigne extract
rows.correct: cyanide can lead to Prussian-blue formation after the appropriate iron-ion treatment
rows.explanation: The procedure requires the specified reagents and suitable acidification.

rows.label: Sulfur with sodium nitroprusside
rows.correct: violet colour
rows.explanation: Sulfide in the fusion extract gives the characteristic response.

rows.label: Nitrogen and sulfur together in sodium fusion
rows.correct: thiocyanate can give a blood-red colour with ferric ions
rows.explanation: The response arises from an iron-thiocyanate complex.

rows.label: Halogen testing in sodium-fusion extract
rows.correct: acidify and boil with nitric acid before adding silver nitrate
rows.explanation: This removes interfering cyanide and sulfide under the prescribed procedure.

rows.label: Silver chloride precipitate
rows.correct: white and soluble in dilute aqueous ammonia
rows.explanation: Complex formation dissolves AgCl under the usual test conditions.

rows.label: Silver bromide precipitate
rows.correct: pale yellow and dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia
rows.explanation: It is less readily dissolved than AgCl.

rows.label: Silver iodide precipitate
rows.correct: yellow and insoluble in aqueous ammonia in the standard test
rows.explanation: Its low solubility resists dissolution in this test.

rows.label: Carbylamine test
rows.correct: primary amines form foul-smelling isocyanides with chloroform and alcoholic KOH
rows.explanation: Secondary and tertiary amines do not give the standard positive test.

rows.label: Neutral ferric chloride with phenol
rows.correct: may produce a characteristic coloured complex
rows.explanation: This is a common test for the phenolic group.

rows.label: 2,4-DNP test
rows.correct: aldehydes and ketones form coloured hydrazone precipitates
rows.explanation: It detects the carbonyl group of these compounds.

rows.label: Tollens test with an aldehyde
rows.correct: silver is deposited from the ammoniacal silver reagent
rows.explanation: The aldehyde is oxidised while silver ions are reduced.

rows.label: Sodium bicarbonate with a carboxylic acid
rows.correct: carbon dioxide effervescence
rows.explanation: A carboxylic acid is strong enough to liberate CO₂ from bicarbonate.

rows.label: Bromine test for alkene unsaturation
rows.correct: bromine colour disappears under the standard addition-test conditions
rows.explanation: Interpret the result with other possible bromine-reactive groups in mind.

rows.label: Carbonate anion with dilute acid
rows.correct: releases carbon dioxide that turns limewater milky
rows.explanation: The gas forms calcium carbonate in limewater.

rows.label: Sulfide anion with dilute acid
rows.correct: can release hydrogen sulfide
rows.explanation: The gas darkens suitable lead-acetate paper by forming lead sulfide.

rows.label: Sulfate with barium chloride after acidification
rows.correct: white barium sulfate precipitate persists in dilute acid
rows.explanation: Acidification helps exclude carbonate interference.

rows.label: Ammonium ion with warm aqueous base
rows.correct: ammonia is released
rows.explanation: The gas turns moist red litmus blue.

rows.label: Copper(II) with excess aqueous ammonia
rows.correct: deep-blue complex solution
rows.explanation: Excess ammonia coordinates to the copper ion.

rows.label: Ferric ion with thiocyanate
rows.correct: blood-red solution under suitable conditions
rows.explanation: A coloured iron-thiocyanate complex forms.

rows.label: Aluminium hydroxide amphoterism
rows.correct: dissolves in both acid and excess strong base
rows.explanation: The hydroxide can form soluble species in either medium.

rows.label: Oxalic-acid versus permanganate titration
rows.correct: warm acidic conditions facilitate the redox reaction
rows.explanation: The standard procedure uses dilute sulfuric acid and appropriate warming.

rows.label: Permanganate titration endpoint
rows.correct: first faint pink colour persisting after mixing
rows.explanation: Permanganate serves as its own indicator. Non-endpoint permanganate is reduced.

rows.label: Strong acid versus strong base titration
rows.correct: equivalence is near pH 7 at 25 °C in the dilute ideal model
rows.explanation: Neutralisation consumes equivalent amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻.

rows.label: Enthalpy of neutralisation of dilute strong acid and base
rows.correct: approximately −57 kJ per mole of water formed
rows.explanation: This approximates H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) forming water.

rows.label: Lyophilic sol preparation
rows.correct: a material with strong affinity for the dispersion medium forms a sol readily
rows.explanation: Starch sols illustrate a lyophilic preparation.

rows.label: Lyophobic sol preparation
rows.correct: a dispersed material with little affinity for the medium requires a suitable preparation method
rows.explanation: Ferric hydroxide sol can be prepared by controlled hydrolysis.

diagrams.explanation: The catalysed forward barrier is 70 − 40 = 30 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the activation barrier without changing reactant and product energies.
